transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, yeah, thank you. Um, well, I guess I'm here because... it's just been a really weird couple of weeks, or maybe longer, I don't even know exactly when it started to get this frustrating. See, I've been trying to, like, really clean up my image and my whole daily routine lately. I got involved with this arts board stuff—which is great, I mean, I really wanted to be part of it because I love community art and I want to put my degree to use, but there's just a lot of pressure to present yourself a certain way, you know? Like you have to look totally put together and be super organized and professional all the time. 

So I tried to do that, to really step up, but ever since I started pushing myself to fit that mold, I’ve just been way more tense and, I don't know, just kind of down than I ever expected to be. It’s like I’m still doing the absolute bare-minimum basics of what I need to do to get by every day, but I keep dropping all these little things that I actually normally really care about. For example, I have these fair planning notes that I was supposed to organize, and my own personal design drafts that I usually love working on, and I just... I keep putting them off or ignoring them completely. 

And then, because I'm not doing them, I feel incredibly guilty. It just sits in the back of my mind all day. So instead of just sitting down and actually catching up on the drafts or the notes, I end up feeling so bad about myself that I just cancel plans with people. I'll just text my friends and make up an excuse because I feel like I shouldn't be going out if I'm behind on everything, but then I stay home and *still* don't do the work. It's just this whole big cycle that I can't seem to get out of, and I just thought I'd be handling this whole arts board thing so much better than I am.
Have you noticed that you’re not enjoying things that you usually like to do, like working on your design drafts or spending time with friends?

Yeah, I guess... I mean, it's not that I don't *like* them anymore, exactly. It's more like I just can't bring myself to do them. Like with the design drafts, usually, I can sit down with my tablet and just get lost in it for hours, you know? I'll put on a playlist, usually something kind of lo-fi or acoustic, and just experiment with colors and layouts. It used to be my favorite way to unwind. But lately, I look at the tablet, and I just feel this heavy, sinking feeling in my stomach. It's almost like the drafts are glaring at me, reminding me of everything I'm not doing right. 

And with my friends, I do want to see them. I miss them! We used to have this standing coffee date on Thursday afternoons at this little place near the park. I'd always get an iced latte, even in the winter, and we'd just talk for hours about whatever. But now, when Thursday rolls around, I just think about how I haven't done my board notes, and how I'm not being the organized, professional person I'm supposed to be, and I just feel like a fraud. I feel like if I go, they'll be able to tell that I'm just faking it, or I'll feel so guilty for having fun when I should be working that I won't even be able to enjoy the coffee anyway. So I just text them and say I have a headache or that I'm too busy with the arts board stuff, which is ironic, because I'm not actually doing the arts board stuff either. I just sit on my couch and stare at the wall and feel terrible about all of it. So I wouldn't say I'm not enjoying them, I'm just... avoiding them, I guess? Because the guilt just ruins it all anyway.

Do you find that activities you used to enjoy, like your design work or time with friends, feel less rewarding or interesting than they used to, or is it more about just not being able to bring yourself to do them?

Yeah, it’s definitely the second one. It’s not like they’ve lost their sparkle or anything, you know? Like, I’m pretty sure if I actually managed to just sit down and do them, I’d still find them totally rewarding. For example, just the other day I was scrolling on my phone and I saw this amazing color palette on Pinterest—it was all these gorgeous muted sage greens and, like, dusty pinks—and my very first thought was immediately, 'Oh wow, I need to try that exact combination for the community center flyer drafts.' So the interest is one hundred percent still there! My brain is still coming up with all these ideas and I still get that little spark of excitement when I see something inspiring. 

It’s just... the bridge between having the idea and actually picking up the stylus to draw is completely broken right now. Because the second I think about actually doing the work, all that pressure I was talking about just comes rushing back in. It’s like this giant wall of guilt. I think, 'Well, you can't just play around with colors right now, you have those official board notes you're supposed to be organizing.' And then I don't do the notes either, obviously. 

But no, I wouldn't say the things themselves are less interesting. Even with my friends, I still want to know what's going on in their lives! I still care if, you know, my friend Sarah's date went well or if Emily got that promotion she was stressing over. I want to be there for all of that, and I know I'd enjoy hearing about it if I could just magically teleport to the coffee shop without all this baggage. It’s purely just that I can’t get past my own head to actually show up. So, yeah, it’s definitely not that I don't care about those things anymore or find them boring, it's just this massive mental block about actually starting them when I feel like I'm failing at this whole new organized, professional version of myself I'm supposed to be.
Have you noticed that you’ve been feeling more tired or lacking energy lately, even if you’re not doing much physically?

I mean, not really? It's not like a physical exhaustion, you know? Like, I'm not waking up feeling like I ran a marathon or anything. I still have the physical energy to, like, get up and make breakfast—usually just oatmeal, I've been trying to eat healthier because I read somewhere that a good breakfast helps with focus, which, ironically, hasn't really worked for me lately—but yeah, I can do the basic physical stuff just fine. I don't feel like I need to sleep for twelve hours a day or anything like that. 

It's more just this... this mental heaviness, I guess? Like, my body is fine, but my brain just feels like it's wading through molasses when I try to think about the arts board stuff or the design drafts. But if you're asking if I'm physically tired or lacking energy in that way, then no, not really. I'm just sitting on the couch because I feel guilty, not because I'm too tired to get off it. If there was an emergency, like if my apartment building caught on fire, I'd definitely have the energy to run down the stairs, you know? It's just... I just don't have the *will* to do the things I'm supposed to be doing. So, yeah, physically, my energy levels are pretty normal, I think.
Have you noticed that you've been feeling down or depressed most of the day, nearly every day, lately?

I wouldn't say I'm depressed most of the day, no. Like, I don't wake up feeling this black cloud over me or anything. It's not this constant, crushing sadness that people always talk about when they talk about being depressed. Actually, my mornings are usually okay. I get up, make my oatmeal, maybe watch a little bit of a YouTube vlog while I eat—lately I've been really into these apartment makeover videos, they're just so satisfying to watch, seeing everything get organized and put in its proper place. It's funny because my own apartment is a mess right now, but watching someone else do it is nice. 

So yeah, during those times, I feel completely normal. I'm not down at all. It's really only when I start thinking about the arts board and all the responsibilities I'm completely failing at that my mood just completely tanks. Like, I'll be fine, and then I'll remember the board notes I haven't filed, or the emails I haven't answered, and suddenly I just feel this intense wave of guilt and inadequacy. And then *that* makes me feel down. But it's very specific to that, you know? If I can distract myself and not think about the board stuff, I actually feel perfectly fine. Like, yesterday afternoon, I spent an hour just organizing my digital reference folders for my art—which isn't actually doing the drafts, I know, it's just moving files around—but I felt totally content while I was doing it. No sadness at all. 

So it's definitely not an "all day, every day" kind of thing. It's more like a roller coaster where the dips only happen when I remember how much I'm messing up this new role. If I could just figure out how to do the work, I don't think I'd feel down at all. It's just the guilt that gets to me, not a general depression, if that makes sense?
Have you noticed that your mood has been low or down more often than not, even if it's not all day every day?

No, honestly, if I had to, like, put it on a pie chart or something, the "feeling down" part would definitely be the smaller slice. It's really not more often than not. Like I was saying with the morning routine and the oatmeal and the YouTube videos—that takes up a good chunk of my day where I feel totally fine. 

And then, you know, in the evenings, my roommate usually comes home around six. She works at this boutique downtown and always has the absolute craziest stories about the customers, so we usually just sit in the kitchen and she vents for like an hour while we figure out dinner. We did tacos last night, actually, with this mango salsa I really wanted to try making from scratch because I had these mangoes that were right on the edge of going bad. And during all of that? I felt totally great. We were laughing, I was chopping onions—well, crying from the onions, obviously, but not like *sad* crying, you know? 

It's really just those specific pockets of the day where I sit down and try to force myself to look at the community center emails, or when I see a notification pop up on my phone from the board president. *That's* when the guilt hits and my mood completely drops. But if you look at the whole day, or even the whole week, the majority of my time is actually pretty okay. I'm just hanging out, doing normal stuff, and feeling mostly like my regular self. It's just that the bad moments feel so incredibly heavy because I'm just so frustrated with myself for not doing what I'm supposed to do. But they definitely don't outnumber the good moments, or even just the neutral, boring moments where I'm just doing laundry or whatever. So no, definitely not more often than not.
Have you found yourself feeling like you're a failure or that you're not good enough, especially in relation to your role on the arts board?

Well, yeah, I guess so. I mean, "failure" is a really strong word, and I don't know if I'd say I'm a failure as a whole person, you know? Like, I'm a good friend, I think. I listen to my roommate when she complains about her job, and I always remember my mom's birthday, and I'm generally a pretty responsible person in most areas of my life. Like, I always pay my half of the rent on time, and I keep the shared spaces in the apartment relatively clean—well, except for right now, like I said, it's a bit messy, but usually, I'm very on top of it. 

But with the arts board... yeah, I definitely feel like I'm completely dropping the ball. It's just so frustrating because I *know* I can do the design work. I have my associate's degree, I've done projects like this before, and I was so excited when they asked me to join the board. It felt like this huge validation, like, "Wow, they actually think my art is good enough to represent the community center." And I had all these ideas for the new promotional materials, like using this really vibrant color palette that reflects the diversity of the neighborhood, and updating the typography to make it look more modern but still approachable. I even started sketching out some concepts in my sketchbook the first week. 

But then... I just stopped. And now, every time I look at those sketches, or every time I see an email from the board president asking for an update, I just feel this massive wave of guilt. And then the guilt turns into this feeling of, like, "Why can't you just do this? What is wrong with you?" It's like I'm proving to them—and to myself, I guess—that I wasn't actually good enough for the role in the first place. Like maybe they made a mistake asking me, and now everyone is going to realize I'm just a fraud who can't even manage a simple volunteer position. 

So, yeah, I definitely feel like I'm failing at *that*. It's just this constant loop in my head of knowing what I need to do, not doing it, and then beating myself up for not doing it. And it's so stupid because it's just a volunteer board, it's not like I'm performing open-heart surgery, but it feels so heavy. I just feel like I'm letting everyone down, especially myself, because I really wanted to be good at this.
Have you had days where you felt down or unmotivated even before getting involved with the arts board or thinking about those responsibilities?

No, definitely not before. I mean, before all this, I was totally fine. Just doing my own thing, making my art, hanging out with my roommate. Honestly, it didn't even start right when I got accepted to the board, either. At first, I was just really excited! 

It actually really started a few weeks after I decided I needed to do this whole... I guess you could call it an "image reset" for the arts board. Because, you know, I looked at the other members, and they're all so established and polished, and here I am, 23, fresh out of my associate's program, usually just wearing vintage band tees and paint-stained overalls. I got it in my head that I wouldn't be taken seriously unless I completely overhauled my life to fit the role. 

So I started changing literally everything. I went out and bought all these structured blazers and these very serious, minimalist monochromatic outfits that are so incredibly uncomfortable and just... not me at all. But I thought, "This is what a board member wears." And I completely changed my routines, too. Instead of just waking up and having my oatmeal and watching my YouTube videos like I like to do, I started forcing myself to get up an hour earlier to go to this really pretentious artisan coffee shop across town, just because I knew the board president and some of the local gallery owners went there. I thought I needed to be seen there, you know? 

And I even changed who I was spending time with. I started blowing off my roommate and my actual friends to go to these incredibly dry networking mixers and these avant-garde gallery openings with people who just talk in circles about, like, the socioeconomic implications of a blank canvas. It was exhausting. 

And it was really only a few weeks into doing all of that—changing my clothes, forcing these new routines, and spending all my time with these new people for this big image reset—that I started feeling this way. That's when that heavy, unmotivated feeling really kicked in and the guilt started piling up. It was like I was trying so hard to be this completely different, "professional" version of myself for the board, and I think it just completely broke my brain. So, yeah, definitely not before the board stuff. It was very specifically tied to me trying to turn myself into someone I'm not for this position.
Have you found that you no longer take pleasure or interest in activities you used to enjoy, even when you manage to do them?

No, not at all. I mean, when I actually just let myself do the things I like, I still really enjoy them just as much as I always have. 

Like, take my art, for example. If I'm sitting there trying to force myself to design those promotional flyers for the community center, I feel absolutely terrible, like my brain is just hitting a brick wall. But if I just sit down to do my own personal stuff? I still love it. Just the other day, I spent probably three hours doing these little watercolor studies of my roommate's houseplants. She has this massive Monstera plant that is literally taking over the entire living room window—seriously, it's like a jungle in there, we had to buy these special moss poles for it and everything so it wouldn't completely collapse on the sofa—and I was just experimenting with mixing these really deep, rich greens using just ultramarine blue and cadmium yellow. And I had the absolute best time! I was totally in the zone, listening to this true crime podcast I've been super into lately about this crazy art heist in the 90s, and I felt completely normal and happy. 

And it's the same with other stuff, too. Like baking or cooking. I still really enjoy that. I mentioned the mango salsa earlier, but last weekend I also made these brown butter chocolate chip cookies because I saw this video on TikTok explaining how browning the butter first gives it this incredible nutty, caramel-like flavor, and honestly, they were amazing. I ate like four of them right off the baking sheet while the chocolate was still all gooey, and my roommate and I just sat on the floor eating cookies and critiquing outfits from this reality show we watch. 

So, yeah, the enjoyment is definitely still there. It's not like the world has gone gray or anything dramatic like that. The things I've always loved, I still love, and I still get a lot of fun out of them. It's really just that specific board stuff and the guilt around it that ruins my mood, but it hasn't, like, poisoned the rest of my hobbies or my life. I still look forward to doing my normal stuff.
Have you noticed that you’ve lost interest or pleasure in almost all activities, even the ones you usually enjoy, most days?

Well, no, like I was just saying, definitely not almost all activities. I mean, it really is just like I mentioned with the watercolors and the baking—most days, as long as I'm not actively agonizing over those community center flyers or forcing myself into one of those stiff blazers, I'm completely fine and I still really love doing my usual stuff. 

Actually, just yesterday, my roommate and I went down to this huge vintage flea market that sets up on the south side of town on the second Sunday of every month. It's usually an absolute nightmare to find parking, like you end up walking six blocks carrying heavy bags, but we actually got a spot right out front this time, which literally never happens. And we spent probably four or five hours just digging through these massive, dusty bins of clothes. I found this amazing, perfectly faded 1980s The Cure t-shirt—which is so rare to find in good condition without paying a fortune—and a pair of these really funky, wide-leg corduroy pants that fit me like an absolute glove. 

And I was so thrilled! I was riding that high all day. I came home and immediately started planning out how I could alter the hem on the pants because I'm a little short, so I dragged out my sewing machine and spent the whole evening just happily pinning and sewing while listening to my music. I didn't feel down or uninterested at all. 

So, yeah, I definitely haven't lost interest in everything most days. If anything, doing those fun things is what keeps me sane right now, because it reminds me of who I actually am when I'm not trying to be this fake, corporate-art-board version of myself. So no, I'm still very much enjoying my life and my hobbies, it's just that one specific dark cloud of the board stuff hanging over me.
Have you had days where you didn’t feel like doing *any* activities—even the ones you usually enjoy—and nothing really seemed interesting or fun?

I feel like I'm kind of repeating myself a bit here, but no, definitely not. There hasn't been a single day where literally nothing sounded fun to me. Even on the days where I'm feeling the absolute most bogged down by all the board responsibilities, I still want to do my own things. 

Like, just this past Tuesday, I was feeling incredibly stressed because I had to draft this formal email to the board president about a budget proposal, which is just so far out of my wheelhouse it's not even funny. But I didn't just sit around staring at the wall feeling dead inside, you know? Instead, I completely abandoned the email and fell down this massive, hours-long rabbit hole on YouTube watching these incredibly detailed video essays about the history of practical special effects in 1980s horror movies. Specifically, like, how they did the transformation scenes in An American Werewolf in London with all those mechanical puppets and the stretching skin and the fake hair. 

It was absolutely fascinating! I was completely engrossed in it, and I even started sketching out some ideas in my notebook because I thought maybe I could incorporate some of those really visceral texture concepts into a new mixed media piece I've been wanting to start. So, yeah, my brain is definitely still very much turned on and engaged when it comes to things I actually care about. It's never just a total blank where nothing sounds good. I always have some weird little project or hyper-fixation going on to keep me entertained, it's really just the forced professional stuff that completely drains me.
Have you had days where you felt down or low even when you weren’t thinking about the arts board or any specific stressors?

No, not really. Honestly, if I'm not thinking about the board or the flyers or all the emails I'm supposed to be sending, I'm completely fine. Like, my mood is totally normal otherwise. 

It's actually kind of funny because my roommate and I were just talking about this. We were sitting on the balcony the other night—we have this tiny little balcony that barely fits two chairs, but we strung up these little solar-powered fairy lights and put out a bunch of potted succulents, so it's actually really cozy—and we were just drinking some tea and talking about how weird it is that I can be having a perfectly great day, totally happy, laughing at stupid memes, and then the second I get a notification on my phone from the board's group chat, it's like a switch flips and my stomach just drops. 

But if that notification doesn't happen? I'm golden. Like on Sundays, I usually turn my phone on 'Do Not Disturb' and just completely ignore the world, and on those days, I don't feel low or down at all. I just putter around the apartment, maybe do some laundry, water the plants, watch a movie... and I feel perfectly content. It's so specifically tied to that one thing. If you took the board completely out of the equation, I don't think I'd be feeling down at all. It's really just that one specific stressor that ruins everything.
Have you had any days where you felt down or low even when you weren’t thinking about the arts board or any other specific stressors?

I know I'm basically a broken record at this point, but no, I really haven't. I mean, you just asked me that, right? Or something really similar? But yeah, the answer is still no. If I'm not thinking about the arts board, I'm just my normal self. 

Like I was saying about Sundays, when I put my phone on 'Do Not Disturb', I'm completely fine. I don't just wake up feeling sad for no reason. It's not like this heavy, mysterious fog that just rolls in out of nowhere and ruins my day, you know? It's very, very specific. 

Actually, it's kind of like... okay, you know when you have a really bad toothache? Like, maybe you need a root canal or something, and it just throbs and throbs. When you're eating ice cream or drinking hot coffee, it's excruciating, right? But if you just sit there and don't agitate it, you're fine. That's exactly how this feels. If I'm just sitting in my apartment, listening to my music, sewing my vintage pants, my 'tooth' doesn't hurt at all. I'm completely happy. But the second I have to think about a budget proposal or look at a community center flyer—bam, the toothache is back and it's all I can think about. 

So, no, there are no days where I just feel down without a reason. It is one hundred percent tied to the board. If the board didn't exist, I'd be having a great time right now. I wouldn't even be sitting here talking to you, honestly. I'd probably be at a thrift store or painting or something. So yeah, definitely not feeling low outside of that one specific, giant headache of a stressor.
Have there been times when you felt down or uninterested in things for two weeks or more at a time, even if you weren't thinking about the arts board or trying to change your routine?

No, never for two weeks straight, and definitely never without it being connected to the board. I feel like we keep circling back to this same idea, but I really want to make sure I'm being clear because I don't want you to think I have some kind of chronic, underlying sadness. I really don't. 

Like, if I look back over the last few months, since all this board stuff started getting really intense, there hasn't been a single block of time—let alone two whole weeks—where I was just walking around in a funk for no reason. Not even close. Even during my absolute worst weeks, when I've had to deal with back-to-back committee meetings and drafting those awful press releases, the bad feelings are always, always broken up by moments where I feel totally like myself again. 

For example, last month was probably the most stressful week I've had so far because we were preparing for the big summer arts festival, and I was in charge of coordinating all the volunteer schedules, which was just a nightmare of spreadsheets and people canceling at the last minute. I was so stressed I was barely sleeping. But even then, in the middle of that horrible week, my friend Sarah came over on a Thursday night and brought this huge container of homemade pad thai, and we just sat on my living room floor eating noodles and watching this terrible reality TV show about people trying to find love while blindfolded or something ridiculous like that. And for those three hours, I was laughing so hard my stomach hurt. I completely forgot about the volunteers and the spreadsheets. I was just happy. 

So, it's never this constant, unbroken stretch of feeling down. It's very episodic, you know? It spikes when I have to deal with the board, and then it drops back down to normal when I can escape it. I've never had a two-week period where I just couldn't shake it, and I've certainly never had a time where I felt that way without the board being the direct cause. If the board isn't bothering me, I'm just living my life, doing my art, hanging out with my friends, and feeling perfectly fine.

Have you ever had a period of time where you felt down or lost interest in almost all activities for most of the day, nearly every day, for a period of two weeks or more, even when you weren’t dealing with the arts board or trying to change your routine?

I feel like we're going in circles a bit here, but no, definitely not. I mean, I really haven't ever had a period like that. Not for two weeks, not for most of the day, and definitely not every day. It's just not how this works for me. 

Like I was trying to explain before, it's so incredibly tied to the board. If I'm not dealing with them, I don't feel down. I don't lose interest in things. I mean, my art is my life. I'm always working on something. Just yesterday, I spent like five hours trying to perfect this new embroidery technique I saw on Pinterest. It's this really intricate floral pattern, and I was so absorbed in it, I completely lost track of time. I didn't even realize how late it was until my roommate came home and asked what was for dinner. I was just so focused and, honestly, really happy doing it. 

If I were feeling down or uninterested in things for two weeks straight, I wouldn't be able to do that, right? I wouldn't care about embroidery or hanging out with my friends or any of the things I normally love. But I do care about those things. I still love them. It's just that when the arts board stuff creeps in, it kind of clouds everything else for a little while. But it always passes once the stressor is gone. 

So, yeah, to answer your question, no. I've never had a two-week period where I felt like that, especially not without the board being the cause. I'm really just a normal, happy person when I'm not drowning in committee emails and budget spreadsheets. I promise I'm not hiding some deep, dark depression from you. It's really just this one specific situation that's messing with me.

Have you ever had a period of time lasting two weeks or more where you felt down or lost interest in most activities most of the day, nearly every day, even when you weren’t dealing with the arts board or trying to change your routine?

Are you... are you reading off a checklist or something? Because I swear you just asked me this exact same thing, almost word for word. I feel like I'm taking crazy pills here! But, um, to answer it again... no. No, I haven't. Not for two weeks, not for one week, not even for three days in a row unless there was some massive crisis happening with the arts board. 

I really don't know how else to explain it so you'll believe me, but I am totally fine when they aren't involved. Like, take my mornings, for example. If I were actually depressed or losing interest in things for two weeks straight, I wouldn't care about my morning routine, right? I'd probably just lay in bed staring at the ceiling. But I don't do that. Every single morning—unless I wake up to some passive-aggressive email from the committee secretary—I get up at 8:30, and I make myself a matcha latte. And I don't just throw powder in a mug and microwave it, I actually do the whole ritual. I use the little bamboo whisk, I froth the oat milk perfectly, I add just a tiny splash of vanilla. It's this whole mindful process that I genuinely look forward to. 

And then I take it over to the window with my cat, Barnaby, and we just watch the birds at this feeder I set up on the fire escape. I actually spent like three days last month just researching the best kind of birdseed to attract goldfinches, because I really wanted to paint them. And it worked! We get so many finches now, and I sit there sketching them for like an hour. If I had lost interest in most activities for most of the day, I wouldn't be doing any of that. I wouldn't care about the finches, I wouldn't care about getting the matcha perfectly smooth, I just wouldn't care. 

But I do care. I love my life, I love my art, I love my little routines. It is literally just the board that drags me down. So, no, absolutely no two-week periods of feeling down for no reason or losing interest in my life. I really, really hope that makes sense this time, because I honestly don't think I can explain it any other way!

Have you ever had a time in your life when you felt down or lost interest in most activities for most of the day, nearly every day, for a period of two weeks or more, even before getting involved with the arts board?

Okay, I see, you're asking about *before* I joined. I mean, I guess I appreciate that we're finally moving off the exact same phrasing, but the answer is still exactly the same. No. Absolutely not. Before I got roped into all this arts board drama, my life was honestly so peaceful and, like, creatively fulfilling. 

I had just finished up my associate's degree, and I was taking some time to figure out my next steps, and I was genuinely so happy. Like, I remember the summer right before I joined the board, I decided to paint this massive mural on the back wall of my parents' garage. It was this huge, intricate underwater scene with all these bioluminescent jellyfish, and I was out there every single day from like ten in the morning until the sun went down. I was using this specific brand of acrylics that dry super fast in the heat, so I had to work really quickly, and I was just covered in blue and purple paint for literally a month straight. I'd be out there listening to my favorite podcasts, just totally in my element, not a care in the world. 

If I had been feeling down or uninterested in things for two weeks back then, there is zero chance I would have been up on a rickety aluminum ladder for eight hours a day trying to get the shading on a sea turtle just right, you know? I wouldn't have had the energy or the motivation. But I was full of energy! I was waking up early, I was going to the farmer's market on weekends to buy fresh peaches, I was dragging my friends over to sit in lawn chairs and watch me paint while we drank iced tea... I was just living a really good, normal, happy life. 

So, no, not before the board, not during the board, not ever. I really, truly have never had a two-week period like what you're describing in my entire life. My baseline is just being a pretty cheerful, creative person. It is 100 percent just this current board situation that's stressing me out, I promise.
Have you ever had a period of time before this arts board situation where you felt down or lost interest in most activities for most of the day, nearly every day, for a period of two weeks or more?

Okay, wait, I... are we glitching? Did the computer freeze or something? Because I literally just answered this exact question. Like, just two minutes ago. I just told you all about the jellyfish mural! 

I really, honestly don't know how many different ways I can say no. The answer is still no. Never. Not before the board, not during, not ever. 

I mean, if you need another example of how totally fine and engaged I was before all this started, I can definitely give you one. Like, right after I got my associate's degree—actually, this was right before I painted the garage—I got super, super into furniture restoration. I found this gorgeous, but completely wrecked, mid-century modern credenza at a thrift store. It was covered in this horrible, thick, gloopy white latex paint. Just completely ruined. And I spent, I kid you not, three entire weeks stripping that paint off.
